clue.text: His "Bonnie" was over the sea, mostly

definitions.text: His "Bonnie" was over the sea, mostly

parts.words: His "Bonnie" was over the sea, mostly
parts.note: points to Bonnie Prince Charlie, the exiled Stuart claimant who spent most of his life abroad, and to the supporter whose hero he was

explanation.surface: A wistful line about a sweetheart who spent most of the time overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonnie' is not a sweetheart but Bonnie Prince Charlie, the Stuart claimant who lived mostly in exile 'over the water'; his followers in the 1745 rising backed him.
explanation.definitionFit: A supporter of the exiled Stuart line, whose figurehead was Bonnie Prince Charlie, living abroad.

clue.text: Dickensian commercial verse

definitions.meaning: Alfred ... is a strolling rogue in Dickens's Pickwick Papers
a catchy rhyme in an advertisement

explanation.definitionFit: A Pickwick Papers character's surname, and a short catchy advertising rhyme.

clue.text: Where gambling is somewhat wrong in company

indicators.note: in says the wrongdoing goes inside the company letters

parts.note: a sin is a piece of wrongdoing

explanation.surface: Gambling happens where a firm behaves rather badly.
explanation.definitionFit: A building or room set aside for games of chance.

clue.text: Began rapid growth, to spur forward in place of retirement

indicators.note: in place of retirement says the spurring words sit inside the bed word

parts.note: a bed is where one retires at night
to urge on is to spur someone forward

explanation.surface: Someone began to grow fast, spurring forward instead of retiring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in place of' looks like 'instead of', but 'in' is the container signal and 'place of retirement' is BED.
explanation.definitionFit: To burgeon is to sprout or flourish quickly.

clue.text: A recent stink created by a striker at court

indicators.note: created suggests the letters are made into something new

explanation.surface: A fresh scandal caused by someone striking at a royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'striker at court' is not a rebel at a palace but the implement that hits a ball on a tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: The strung bat used to strike the ball on a tennis court.

clue.text: One has a doctor in charge with such feet

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: Someone sees a doctor in charge about their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feet' are not body parts but metrical feet in verse; an iamb is a short syllable then a long one.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse built on iambs, the metrical unit of an unstressed then a stressed syllable, is described this way.

clue.text: Included in a team on genetics

indicators.note: included says the letters are contained within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone is included in a team working on genetics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Included' signals the run sitting inside 'team on genetics'; the lone 'in' is the definition, as in 'in their number'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean in the midst of or in the company of others.

clue.text: Like certain rocks, as found in the sea

indicators.note: found in says the little word sits inside the sea's name

parts.note: the Baltic is a sea of northern Europe

explanation.surface: Description of rocks as they are found in the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Of basalt, the dark volcanic rock.

clue.text: About a literary rogue producing fruit

parts.note: C, for circa, means about
Rogue Herries is a novel by Hugh Walpole about Francis Herries

explanation.surface: A tale about a rogue in literature that bears fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Small round stone fruits, red or black.

clue.text: Owl's bob's-worth from a pig

parts.note: recalls Edward Lear's poem in which the Owl buys from a Piggy-wig, for one shilling, the ring at the end of its snout; a bob is slang for a shilling

explanation.surface: A nonsense purchase: an owl buying a shilling's worth of something from a pig.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lear's The Owl and the Pussy-cat, the pig sells its ring for one shilling, and 'bob' is old British slang for a shilling.
explanation.definitionFit: The ornament in the Piggy-wig's snout, sold to the Owl for a shilling in Lear's poem.

clue.text: Ruffle almost all the French

indicators.note: almost signals that the final letter of the French phrase is left off

parts.note: tous les is French for all the

explanation.surface: Someone ruffles very nearly all the French people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the last S of TOUS LES.
explanation.definitionFit: To dishevel or rumple hair, as one would ruffle it.

clue.text: Relatives of King George and many others

parts.note: GR, Georgius Rex, is King George's royal cipher
taken as written
M, a thousand in Roman numerals, stands for many
taken as written

explanation.surface: The relatives of King George and many other people.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandparents on the female side are family relatives.

clue.text: Forward thrust by toboggan round the pole

indicators.note: round says the toboggan word goes around the pole letter

parts.note: a luge is a small racing toboggan
N stands for the North pole

explanation.surface: A tobogganist thrusts forward on a run around the polar region.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden forward thrust, as in fencing.

clue.text: Pull back into rear one right in front, being out of order

indicators.note: in front says these two letters go at the start of the rest

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: into says the turned word is put inside the rear word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back tells us the word for pull is read from right to left

parts.note: to lug is to pull or drag

explanation.surface: Instructions to pull someone back into the rear with one right at the front, all out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull' looks like the action, but it is just the word to reverse; 'out of order' is the definition, with 'being' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not following the usual rule or sequence is not in proper order.

clue.text: Passing through I have appeared to be without object

parts.note: a traveller passing through is in transit
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A traveller passing through seems to have no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'object' is a grammatical object, not a purpose: a verb taking no direct object.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar term for a verb that takes no direct object.

clue.text: Hot-tempered product of a strange Carib isle

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters form an odd new order

explanation.surface: Someone hot-tempered was born on a strange Caribbean island.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick to anger.

clue.text: Mrs Mopp has children of divine grace

parts.note: Mrs Mopp, the cleaning lady in the BBC radio comedy ITMA, is a char or charwoman
someone with children is a ma, a mother

explanation.surface: A cleaning woman with children has a heavenly gift.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is a British charwoman, a cleaner; Mrs Mopp was the char in the 1940s radio show ITMA. 'has children' reads as 'is ma'.
explanation.definitionFit: In theology, a gift or power bestowed by God; now a compelling personal appeal.

clue.text: It's of no great account in Vienna

definitions.text: It's of no great account in Vienna

parts.words: It's of no great account in Vienna
parts.note: describes a small Austrian coin of little value; the first syllable is German for great, hence 'no great' value

explanation.surface: Something that doesn't matter much in Vienna.
explanation.walkthrough: It was the hundredth part of the Austrian schilling; its name comes from Latin grossus, thick or big, so 'no great account' is a play on that.
explanation.definitionFit: Small Austrian coin worth one hundredth of a schilling.

clue.text: Smith Minor's French charger out of action?

definitions.meaning: a schoolboy, the younger Smith, would render a war-horse in French by this phrase, reading the first word as 'horse'

explanation.walkthrough: Smith Minor is the younger of two Smith brothers at a British school; his schoolboy French takes 'hors' for 'horse' and 'combat' for battle, giving a warhorse.
explanation.definitionFit: French phrase used in English for a combatant disabled and no longer fighting.

clue.text: Light blue taxi with a sort of tan interior

indicators.note: interior says the jumbled letters go inside the taxi word

parts.note: a cab is a taxi

indicators.note: sort of suggests the letters of tan are made into a version of themselves

explanation.surface: A pale blue taxi whose interior has a tan sort of colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges TAN into NTA, and with A that makes the 'interior' of CAB. Light blue is Cambridge University's colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cambridge man or woman, from the university's colour of light blue.

clue.text: Much fuddled, my friends usually are

indicators.note: fuddled means confused, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: My friends are usually rather drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Friendly and intimate, as pals tend to be.

clue.text: Official matter, pressing, is rising up again

parts.note: res is the Latin word for a thing or matter, used in legal and official language
a pressing need is an urgent one

explanation.surface: A pressing official matter keeps coming back.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming back to strength or prominence after a decline, as a revived movement does.

clue.text: Notice zero hour coming up for her

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: an ad, advertisement, is a notice
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A notice that zero hour is approaching for her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming up' reverses ADOHR, read bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's name, so a 'her'.

clue.text: A pound, money, down, causes conflict

indicators.note: down here means set down within, so the pound letter is put inside the money word

parts.note: cash is money
L, from libra, is the abbreviation for a pound

explanation.surface: Paying down a pound in cash leads to an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: To clash is to come into conflict or disagree.

clue.text: This tie forms a bond, if old

definitions.text: This tie forms a bond, if old

parts.words: This tie forms a bond, if old
parts.note: the old ... tie worn by former pupils, a phrase for the network of favours among those educated together

explanation.surface: A remark that a necktie creates friendship, provided it is old.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'old school tie' is a British symbol of the loyalty between people from the same (usually private) school.
explanation.definitionFit: Place of education whose former pupils wear the old tie as a badge of belonging.

clue.text: Uncommonly brave little boy, so quoted

indicators.note: uncommonly suggests the letters of brave are arranged in an unusual way

parts.note: Tiny Tim is the little boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol, and Tim a short boy's name

explanation.surface: A remarkably brave little boy is quoted.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeated word for word, exactly as quoted.

clue.text: Trojan did love the queen he deserted

definitions.text: Trojan did love the queen he deserted

parts.words: Trojan did love the queen he deserted
parts.note: describes the hero of Virgil's epic, who loved Dido, queen of Carthage, then left her to found Rome

explanation.surface: A Trojan really did love the queen he walked out on.
explanation.definitionFit: Virgil's Trojan hero abandoned Dido of Carthage after their love affair.

clue.text: Legislative body takes a line in industrial production

definitions.meaning: the putting together of parts in a factory, as on a production line

explanation.definitionFit: A law-making council, and the fitting together of components in manufacturing.
